shortQuestions: I agree with the writer: gender inequality is rooted in social customs and attitudes rather than in religion; denying women education, health care and economic opportunities harms not only women but the whole society's progress. (Students may give their own reasoned view.)

Many Pakistani women, especially in rural areas, lack proper health care: high maternal and infant mortality, malnutrition and anaemia, early marriages, lack of trained midwives and lady doctors, and neglect of girls' health compared with boys. Social restrictions and poverty also keep them from reaching hospitals.

Factors include low literacy and lack of skills, early marriage, social customs that limit women's work outside the home, denial of inheritance and property rights, unequal wages, lack of safe transport and workplaces, and limited access to loans and business opportunities.

Islam gives women dignity and equal human worth: "O mankind! We created you from a single male and female" (49:13); men and women get equal reward for good deeds (4:124). Women have rights of education, property, inheritance (4:7), mahr, consent in marriage and kind treatment — the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "The best of you are those who are best to their wives" and "Seeking knowledge is obligatory on every Muslim."

Example: in my area girls are often withdrawn from school after the primary level while boys continue to college; or at home sons get better food and freedom than daughters. (Students describe an incident they have observed.)

The motive is to make readers aware of gender inequality and its harmful effects on women and society, and to urge people and the government to give women their rights in education, health and economic life in the light of Islam.

Suggestions: free and compulsory education for girls; awareness campaigns about women's Islamic rights; strict implementation of laws on inheritance, harassment and early marriage; better health facilities and lady health workers; vocational training and jobs for women; equal pay; and changing attitudes through media and religious scholars.
activities: Sample argumentative essay — The bread earner has always got a stronger social status: Introduction — In most societies the person who earns money for the family enjoys more respect and authority. Arguments — First, money gives power to make decisions, so the earner controls the family budget. Second, society values paid work more than unpaid work such as housework and child care. Third, economic independence gives confidence and freedom. Counter-argument — However, Islam and good sense teach that status should depend on character and contribution, not income; the mother's role in raising children is as valuable as earning. Conclusion — It is true that the bread earner has usually enjoyed a stronger status, but a just society should honour every member's contribution and give women equal opportunities to earn.

Debate guide — For women equality: equal rights in Islam, education, economic participation and national progress, examples of successful women. Against (as debate practice): traditional roles, family responsibilities, cultural values. Each speaker gets two minutes; the teacher concludes with the Islamic view of justice and dignity for women.
